full_judgment:
4. On these pleadings the parties fought out the suit. The court of first instance on a consideration of the pleadings of the parties and the evidence on record came to the view that the Hiba deed was not fraudulently obtained from their father when he was in an unconscious state of mind but it was executed by their father voluntarily and at his free will knowing the contents of the same. In that view of the matter the suit of the plaintiff was dismissed on contest with costs. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge concurring with the finding of fact arrived at by the court of first instance dismissed the appeal with costs. The judgment and decree of the learned Munsif were affirmed. As against that the decrees of affirmance the plaintiff has preferred this appeal to this court. Mr. Md. Nurul Haq, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal having taken me through the judgment of both the courts below and the evidence on record has urged that both the courts below erred In coming to finding of fact as to the execution of the Hiba deed on a misreading of the evidence on record so also as to the due execution and proper presentation of the same before the Registrar by the executant himself on the basis of no evidence at all. He has further urged that the courts below erred in not holding that in the absence of any proper proof of the existence of the essential ingredience of a valid gift mere registration would not make it valid and this legal aspect of the matter has escaped the attention of both the courts below and it has caused an error affecting the merits of the case. He has lastly urged that the courts below had also erred in not holding that the alleged Hiba deed was executed during the Murz-ul-Maut or death illness making the gift a will. This legal aspect of the matter had also not been considered by the courts below. 

 8. There is a presumption of good faith in transaction and he who alleges bad faiths such as fraud need to prove the same. Further in-the instant case it was the plaintiff who was pleading affirmative of the issues No.3 namely, that it was a case of fraud and he who pleads affirmative of the issue also need to prove the same. Further, it was the plaintiff who wishes the court to believe in the existence or non- existence of a material fact. It was thus for him to prove the non- existence of that material fact namely, the non-existence of Hiba in the eye of law and further if no evidence was led on either side it would be the plaintiff who would lose. Therefore, on all counts, it was for the plaintiff to prove the fraudulent character of the deed and this he cannot prove by the weakness, if any, in defence testimony. In an attempt to prove the fraudulent character of the Hiba deed the plaintiff examined a number of witnesses and they stated that on that very day i e. on 29th Chaitra, 1374 B.S. the old man was taken in a bier to Chandpur while he was in a senseless condition but the plaintiff gave a go-bye to those as he came up with the story that his father's thumb impression were taken in stamp papers by the defendant on the plea that those would be required for admission in the hospital. It is not understood as to why it need to be stated so by the defendant if his father was in a senseless state of mind and why it would be required .to explain to him the reasons for taking his thumb impression if he was senseless. It is thus apparent that the old man was not in a senseless condition but he was in a position to understand and understand the reason and effect of putting his thumb impression on any paper whether ordinary paper or on stamp paper. Further the plaintiff asserted that those were taken on the plea that those would be required for admission in the hospital without disclosing the source of his knowledge or as to the basis or the said testimony as admittedly the plaintiff came only after the death of old man and he knew nothing as to what had happened when the old man was at Chandpur. All these he allegedly heard from others and those hearsay evidence cannot go into evidence to prove the correctness of the fact to the effect that his father was taken to Chandpur in a senseless state of mind when he was unable to understand. Further it is seen that the alleged fraudulent Bibadeed was registered by the Sub-Registrar, Chandpur on 29th Chaitra, 1374 B.S. On a reference to the said document it is seen that not only the stamp papers for the alleged Hiba deed were personally purchased by the said old man on 29.12./4 B.S. but that it was he who had presented the Hiba deed for registration as its executant before the Registrar. There is an endorsement of the Register to the effect that the executant Abdul Jabbar Karl @ Jabbar Ali admitted the execution of the deed before the Registrar and he was identified by Md. Fazlur Rahman in his presence. The registration of a deed is a solemn act performed by a competent officer appointed for the purpose. Under the provisions of the Registration Act, every document need to be registered must be presented for registration by the persons executing the said document or by the persons claiming under the same or by representative or assigns of such persons executing or by an agent duly authorised in that regard, After they said was presented by a proper per son to the satisfaction of the register, the registering officer would be under a duty to enquire whether or not such document was in fact executed by the persons by whom it purports to have been executed after satisfying himself as to the identity of the persons appearing before him admitting that he had executed the document. When all those formalities as required under sections 3435, 58 and 59 as referred to earlier have been complied with, the registering officer shall endorse there on a certificate containing the word "registered" and the said shall then be admissible for the purpose of proving that" the document has been duly registered and that the facts mentioned in the endorsement have occurred as therein mentioned. This being the legal position a document when registered it would be assumed that the document was explained to the executant before registration who admitted in execution and the receipt of consideration and that the whole proceeding and endorsement were regular and in order. It would also be an evidence of the fact of presentation of the document for registration before the registering authority by the person so recorded and also be an evidence of the fact of the person being properly identified by the identifier as mentioned in the deed to the satisfaction of the registering authority. Keeping in mind this legal effect and evidentiary value of a registered document It is to be understood as to how if the plaintiff's deceased father was in a senseless state it could have been possible for him either to purchase the stamp for the same from the vendor personally or to present it before the Registrar personally for registration and to admit its execution before the registering authority, when under the law registration of a document would be an evidence of execution of the same. It is true that mere registration of a document would not and could not be regarded as sufficient proof of voluntary execution or that it was done while in sound mind. It there exists circumstances which would lend support to any plea of non-voluntarily execution it would be incumbent upon the court to proceed with great caution and to avoid arriving at a finding of fact as to voluntary execution or execution while of sound mind merely on the basis of the fact that the deed was a registered document. In the instant case there however, exists no such suspicious circumstance and proof to substantiate the plaintiff's claim that his father being senseless was incapable of executing the alleged Hiba deed no the 29th Chaitra, 1374 B S. Some of the plaintiff's witnesses stated that the old man was taken to Chandpur in a bier in a senseless condition and in spite of their protest without disclosing the source of their knowledge as to his being in a senseless condition. Mere opinion would not prove a fact. The legal presumption that exists as to due execution of a registered document needs to be rebutted by very strong evidence and not merely by hearsay evidence as to the senseless condition of the old man. In the case of Gangamoyi Debi Vs. Troiluckhya Nath Chowdhury and another reported in 33 Indian Appeals, at page 60. Sir Ford North ill delivering the judgment of the judicial committee of the Privy Council on similar matters observed thus: 

 "The document was registered and, having regard to the observation of their Lordships of .the Privy Council in Gongamoyi Debi Vs. Troiluckhya Nath Chowdhury (1) and Baijnath Singh V. Jamal Bros & Co. Ltd, (2), we may take it that the document was explained by Sub-Registrar to the executants who admitted its execution and the receipt of consideration and that the whole proceedings in connection with registration and endorsement, etc. were regular and in order. In any event the burden of proof was upon the plaintiffs to show that the document was without consideration". 

 10. I am in respectful agreement with the observation as above which are in complete accord with the view I have taken hereinbefore to the effect that the endorsement of the Registrar would be a strong presumptive evidence of the fact that the document was explained to the executant who admitted his execution and the receipt of consideration and that the whole proceeding and the endorsement made therein were regular and in order and they said could only be rebutted by the plaintiff by adducing strong evidence proving the allegation that the executant was not in his senses at the time of the execution of the deed or any fraud was committed upon the sub Registrar by an imposter. That would again be a question of fact and it would be futile to argue such in the circumstance of the case when there was none who could depose from his personal knowledge as to the fact of the old man being actually senseless although from the time he was taken to Chandpur till the registration. It has been urged by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the courts below failed to take into consideration that the existence of the essential ingredient of a valid gift by a Muslim had not been proved by the defendant who was claiming title under the said document. In elaborating the point he argued further by contending that in order to constitute a. valid gift under the principal of Mohammadian Law there must exist a Clear intention or a declaration made by the donor expressing his intention to make the gift followed by delivery of' possession of the corpus and acceptance of the same by the donee. On a reference to the registered Hiba deed it is seen that it had been clearly recited in that deed that the donor had executed the document clearly gifting away the property mentioned on free will without any coercion and he did the same understanding the consequences and while in sound mind. It. is true that registration of a document would prove its registration and due execution only and not the truth or otherwise of the contents or the recitals appearing in the document. These need to be proved if challenged to be incorrect both as to title and as to delivery of possession. Though registration itself would not conclusively prove the truth of the contents of a document yet the recitals in a document, admitted by the executants before the Registrar would create a rebuttable presumption as to correctness of the facts stated therein and the onus would lie upon the party alleging otherwise as there exists a general presumption of good faith and legality in all human transactions. In the instant case there is nothing on record to show that the plaintiff have been able to discharge that burden by proving that in fact no such declaration was made in the deed of gift at his free will and that no possession of the property gifted was handed over, Rather it is admitted that the defendant is in possession of the whole property and only on village salish he handed back plaintiff's share which was totally denied by the defendant. The said, however, was not an issue framed before any of the courts below and no evidence led to that effect and rightly it has been urged by the learned Advocate for the respondents that the plaintiff could not be allowed to go beyond his pleadings and go beyond the issues framed and to raise a new point based essentially on facts in Second Appeal. The said has substance and needs to be sustained.
